newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Lev plunges as Bulgarians rush for dollars.
newsitem.headline: Lev plunges as Bulgarians rush for dollars.

text.p: The Bulgarian lev fell 18 percent on the day to close at another all-time low of 390-395 per dollar on Thursday as Bulgarians rushed to convert their savings into dollars.
Shopkeepers in the capital Sofia raised their prices for imported goods every hour, and frequently asked for payment in dollars or marks, though this is barred by law.
"Suppliers are asking for payment in foreign currency and that's illegal, so we're not doing any business," said one foreign businessman.
The fall will further fuel inflation, which was a monthly 16.7 percent in October, reaching 195.1 percent since the beginning of the year.

"The market was very nervous and confused and every dollar on offer was grasped, irrespective of the exchange rate," a commercial bank dealer said. Traders said business was very thin in the afternoon as foreign currency supply was almost nil.

Central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov said on Wednesday the bank would continue to support the lev as much as it could but it could not deplete its reserves to counter a highly speculative dollar rush.
Dealers said the central bank was not seen selling dollars in the market on Thursday.
The central bank board adjourned its weekly meeting on Thursday evening. A spokesman said it would continue on Friday but no comment was available on the lev decline.
Many exchange bureaus stopped selling dollars as they were unsure what rate to use. A rumour swept the foreign exchange market that the bureaus would be closed to limit dollar sales.

The lev began the week at 272-275 on Monday. Businessmen at foreign companies said they were watching developments with great concern. "We'll still continue to do business but pricing is a bit of a problem," said one.

Politicians and bankers are discussing an International Monetary Fund proposal for a currency board to stabilise the economy by forcing Bulgaria to match levs in circulation with foreign exchange reserves.

Reaction to the proposal has been mixed. While many traders say they would welcome a more predictable exchange rate, the central bank fears a loss of sovereignty, and some businessmen fear it could dry up trade by causing an initial shortage of foreign currency.
Details of how a currency board would work have yet to be settled, and the question of who should run it and how much independence it will be allowed has attracted much speculation.
Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov favours running it out of the existing central bank.
Panicked depositors have withdrawn some 14.4 billion levs since last week from the State Savings Bank, the country's largest savings institution.
Some 75 percent of its deposits are invested in Treasury paper and depositors feared the finance ministry might suspend payments on government securities under a currency board.

Payments of $300 million on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt fall due in the first quarter of 1997 and debt markets speculate that Bulgaria could become the first country to default on a Brady debt restructuring deal.
BNB foreign exchange reserves reserves stood near $541 million at the end of October, down from $1.434 billion a year ago. The central bank also manages gold reserves worth some $400 million.
Bulgaria has the lowest rate of foreign investment in the region and has lagged behind other countries in implementing structural reforms since the end of communist rule in 1989.
